summary: This experimental document specifies a point-to-point route discovery mechanism that complements the core Routing Protocol for Low-power and Lossy Networks (RPL). It lets an IPv6 router discover routes on demand to other routers in a low-power and lossy network, meeting specified metric constraints.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny sensor networks can ask "find me a good path to that device," instead of always using one fixed route.

questions: on-demand routes in low-power lossy networks
how does rpl point-to-point route discovery work
subtitle: How a router in a low-power wireless network can find a good route to another router on demand, instead of detouring through the DAG root.

tldr.problem: In core RPL, two routers that are not the root can only talk along links of the DAG, so routes must be set up ahead of time and may be long and congest the root.
tldr.mechanism: The Origin builds a short-lived DAG rooted at itself using DIO messages in a new P2P Route Discovery mode. Each DIO accumulates a route, and the Target sends the chosen route back in a P2P-DRO message.
tldr.outcome: The discovered routes are guaranteed to meet the stated metric constraints but may not be the best. The RFC is Experimental, and the authors expected a later revision for the Standards Track.

facts.label: Routes per Target
facts.value: 1 hop-by-hop or up to 4 source routes

today: RFC 6997 is an Experimental specification and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says it was published for evaluation and anticipated a revision for the Standards Track once operational experience was gained.

sections.title: Why On-Demand Point-to-Point Routes
sections.content:
The IPv6 Routing Protocol for Low-power and Lossy Networks (RPL, RFC 6550) builds a DAG rooted at one router. When two other routers want to talk, their packets may only travel along links in that DAG. The RFC lists two problems for home and building automation: every destination must declare itself ahead of time, and routes restricted to the DAG can be badly suboptimal and cause congestion near the DAG root.

Use cases include a remote control that suddenly needs to reach a lamp whose address it knows, and large building networks where traffic among hundreds or thousands of routers jams the root. P2P-RPL lets a router discover routes to one or more other routers on demand. The routes are not necessarily the best but are guaranteed to meet the specified metric constraints, which makes them good enough for the application.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally everyone has to send messages through the one boss in the middle, which gets crowded. This lets two friends find a shortcut to each other only when they need it.

sections.title: How a Route Discovery Works
sections.content:
The Origin starts a discovery by forming a temporary DAG rooted at itself. The DIO messages that build it use a new Mode of Operation, P2P Route Discovery mode, with value 4. Each such P2P mode DIO carries exactly one P2P Route Discovery Option (P2P-RDO) naming the Target, whether hop-by-hop or source routes are wanted, how many routes, and whether the Target should reply. The RDO also carries the best route from the Origin that the sending router has seen so far.

As routers join the temporary DAG they append their own address to the route and re-advertise it. A router discards a DIO whose accumulated metrics break the listed constraints, so constraints also limit how far the DIOs travel. When the Target receives a DIO, it holds a complete source route from the Origin. If the Origin asked for replies, the Target sends a P2P-DRO back, carrying one discovered route per message.

The scheme discovers either one hop-by-hop route or up to four source routes per Target. The temporary DAG exists only to find routes and MUST NOT be used to route data packets. The installed routes outlive the DAG for their own lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: You shout a request that spreads out through the room, and every helper adds their name to the note before passing it on. When it reaches your pal, the note is a full path from you to them.

sections.title: The Route Discovery Option and Reply Messages
sections.content:
The P2P-RDO has option type 0x0a. Its flags and fields are R (reply allowed), H (hop-by-hop routes if one, source routes if zero), N (number of source routes wanted, minus one), Compr (prefix octets elided from addresses) and L, a 2-bit lifetime that says how long every router must stay in the temporary DAG: 1, 4, 16 or 64 seconds. A MaxRank field caps the rank a router may have, and a TargetAddr and an Address vector hold the target and the route accumulated so far, in forward order, without the Origin and Target themselves.

The P2P-DRO (control code 0x04, secure version 0x84) carries the RPLInstanceID, Version, DODAGID and one P2P-RDO holding the complete route. Its S flag (Stop) tells routers that discovery is over so they should stop generating or processing DIOs for that temporary DAG. Its A flag asks the Origin for an acknowledgement, and a 2-bit sequence number pairs the two. Travelling back, a P2P-DRO moves hop by hop along the route, and for a hop-by-hop route each router stores the next-hop state as it passes.

The P2P-DRO-ACK (code 0x05, secure 0x85) is unicast from the Origin to the Target. If the Target does not see it within P2P_DRO_ACK_WAIT_TIME it may resend, up to MAX_P2P_DRO_RETRANSMISSIONS times.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has boxes to fill in: who you want, how many paths, and how long everyone should keep listening. The reply note carries the finished path, and a thank-you note can confirm it arrived.

sections.title: Rules for Routers During Discovery
sections.content:
The Origin sets the DIO base fields in a fixed way: Version Number zero, Grounded flag one, Mode of Operation four, DODAGPreference zero, and the DODAGID set to an address of the Origin. MaxRankIncrease must be zero, which disables local repair, and the Authentication Enabled flag must be zero. If no DODAG Configuration Option is present, defaults apply, including DIOIntervalMin of 6 (64 ms), DIORedundancyConstant of 1 and Objective Function Zero.

A router drops a P2P mode DIO if it has INFINITE_RANK, if its rank reaches the MaxRank limit, if the metrics break a mandatory constraint, or if a P2P-DRO with the Stop flag was already seen for that DAG. An Intermediate Router also drops it if received on an ingress-only interface, or if adding its address would put it in the route twice. Links are expected to have bidirectional reachability, so the Target can use the route in reverse.

DIOs are sent under a Trickle timer. A first-heard DIO or one that lets the router advertise a better route counts as inconsistent and resets the timer. The recommended redundancy constant is 1, and Imin should be at least an order of magnitude above the typical DIO transmission delay in highly connected networks. A Target that is the only target MUST NOT forward the DIO further, and it MAY set the Stop flag once it has the routes it wants.

To reuse an RPLInstanceID safely the Origin should wait about twice the L duration, or, for the same Target, X plus twice the L duration where X is the route state lifetime.
sections.plainLanguage: There are house rules: helpers ignore notes that are too long, too bad or loop back to them, and they stop passing notes once someone shouts that the job is done.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content:
Each RPL control message has a secure version, marked by a 1 in the most significant bit of the Code. For P2P-RPL the Origin decides whether to use security and which Security Configuration to use, and every participating router MUST follow it. The Origin MUST NOT use Key Identifier Mode 1, a per-pair key, because messages travel by multicast or over multiple hops. A router that sees mixed secure and unsecure DIOs, or a configuration it cannot use, MUST NOT join. A router that later sees a message not matching its remembered configuration enters a lock down mode and stops generating or processing messages for that discovery.

A rogue router holding the key could advertise false routes, forge or alter P2P-DROs, or, acting as Origin, start fake discoveries as a denial of service. Because source routes are involved, the RFC notes that concerns behind the deprecation of Type 0 routing headers may apply, so each Intermediate Router checks the route for loops.

P2P-RPL generally does not affect core RPL, but an RPL router that does not understand the new mode may join the temporary DAG as a leaf and keep memory state after the DAG is gone. The mechanism works best when all RPL routers implement it.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone must use the same secret handshake the starter picked. If someone uses a different one, their neighbors ignore them, so a troublemaker cannot easily spoil the search.
